title: segresearch: where byte-level language models should start their patches
abstract: Code, logs and results for the paper Easy to anticipate, hard to compute: boundary dependence finds the computed outputs that entropy patching misses. Byte-level language models such as BLT start a patch where next-byte entropy is high; under tight budgets this skips positions whose type is predictable but whose value must be computed, such as the number after '=' in a worked math solution. The repository contains the BLT-style training harness (MLX, and a PyTorch port verified against it), the experiments on Meta's BLT-1B (with the upstream fix for the 512-byte attention window of the Hugging Face conversion), the scaling study at 1M-50M parameters, the results registry with per-target outputs, and the scripts that regenerate every table, figure and tested number of the paper. Datasets (GSM8K, MATH, OpenWebMath) and the BLT-1B weights are not redistributed; the scripts download them from their sources.

title: AI自主创作拟人化认知污染假说——人机交互创作权属与原生创新边界研究
abstract: 摘 要 当前社会普遍存在“AI可自主创作、AI可独立写论文、AI可原创假说”的主流认知。该观点默认人工智能具备自主思考、问题发现与理论创新能力。本文通过纯思想实验与逻辑公理推演,证明:大众所谓“AI自主创作”并非机器原生智能产出,而是人类对人机交互结果的拟人化认知污染错觉。 AI所有高阶输出(理论、假说、学术观点、体系架构、创新性文本)完全依赖人类前置输入的问题意识、框架约束、逻辑边界与原创构想。AI仅承担文本规整、逻辑延伸、去口语化、内容重组的拟合加工工作,不具备从零生成可证伪、自洽、全新公理体系的原生创新能力。 本文建立可量化、可证伪的创作边界公式,给出唯一严格证伪实验标准,彻底区分「机器文本拟合」与「人类原生思想创新」,厘清人工智能创作的真实权属边界,纠正当前人工智能传播中的普遍性认知偏差。

title: Vous avez dit "intelligence artificielle" ?
abstract: Ce cours a été préparé en 2024, pour les étudiant·es de Licence de Biologie à l'Université Paris Saclay. Il a pour objectif d'introduire la notion "d'intelligence artificielle". En particulier, il présente la différence entre algorithmes symbolique et "machine learning". Des ressources sont également partagées, afin de permettre une appropriation des concepts fondamentaux en lien avec "l'IA".

title: A GRU-Augmented Kalman Filter for State Estimation in Systems with Colored Noise
abstract: Although the Kalman filter is optimal for linear Gaussian systems, its performance degrades in practical scenarios when noise is colored rather than white. Additionally, the Kalman filter requires substantial domain knowledge to derive parametric forms. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a data-driven filtering method that operates in the presence of colored noise and with partial information without requiring exact prior knowledge. We propose CKFNet, a novel real-time filtering framework that integrates a linear state-space model under colored noise with a gated recurrent unit. The network replaces the traditional Kalman gain computation, enabling the model to implicitly learn noise statistics from data and adapt to colored noise dynamics. Experiments across various colored noise conditions and model mismatch scenarios show that CKFNet outperforms baseline methods in most tested scenarios, and remains robust where model-based filters degrade. The results indicate that CKFNet effectively combines the interpretability and efficiency of state-space models with the adaptive learning capability of neural networks, offering a reliable filtering solution under realistic noise assumptions.

title: Analisis Pengaruh Ukuran Chunk terhadap Kinerja Retrieval-Augmented Generation pada Tanya Jawab Dokumen Akademik
abstract: Evaluasi otomatis sistem tanya jawab berbasis Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) dapat menyesatkan ketika pertanyaan ujinya dibuat secara sintetis. Pertanyaan yang diturunkan dari blok teks berukuran tetap cenderung menaikkan skor konfigurasi pembagian teks (chunking) yang menggunakan ukuran yang sama. Penelitian ini membandingkan empat ukuran potongan teks, yaitu 128, 256, 512, dan 1024 token pada sistem tanya jawab Buku Panduan Akademik Universitas Muhammadiyah Purwokerto (UMP) yang dibangun dengan Structure-Aware Recursive Splitter, model embedding BAAI/bge-m3, dan generator gpt-oss-120b. Performa diukur dengan kerangka RAGAS pada 950 pertanyaan sintetis dan 51 pertanyaan organik (buatan manusia); hanya hasil pada dataset organik yang diuji dengan Wilcoxon Signed-Rank serta koreksi Holm. Skenario 512 token unggul pada seluruh metrik di dataset sintetis, konsisten dengan kebocoran data struktural. Keunggulan tersebut tidak terulang pada pertanyaan organik: tidak ditemukan perbedaan signifikan di antara skenario 256, 512, dan 1024 token (), dan hasil ini belum dapat disimpulkan karena daya statistik yang rendah ( hingga 41). Skenario 512 token layak dijadikan pilihan awal yang hemat sumber daya karena memerlukan sekitar separuh beban konteks inferensi skenario 1024 token tanpa perbedaan kualitas jawaban yang terdeteksi pada kondisi yang diuji.

title: From Prototype to Massing: Learning Graph Correspondence for Scalable Facade Modeling
abstract: Facade articulation at building scale is usually resolved manually or through parametric systems that encode design intent as explicit rules. This paper investigates a complementary workflow in which a designer-authored prototype supplies transferable articulation logic. Prototype and target massing are represented as heterogeneous attributed graphs, and a Siamese graph attention network with instance-local triplet supervision embeds their segments in a shared metric space. Many-to-one nearest-neighbor retrieval then routes prototype Patterns to the larger target. On the original 85/15 within-corpus holdout, prototype-to-massing top-1 accuracy reached 96.5%, compared with a reported 76.5% raw-feature baseline. A Rhino demonstrator converts predicted correspondence into reusable facade Patterns, and qualitative applications on four built projects show the workflow across distinct massing organizations. The contribution is not automated facade generation, but an authoring model in which resolved geometry serves as a computational specification for project-scale propagation.

title: GlucoPRISM: Protocol-Supervised Pretraining for Cross-Cohort Glucose Transfer
abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) foundation models encode each day as one vector that mixes who the person is, what happened that day and how the sensor measured it, so measurement differences travel with the representation into new cohorts. We ask whether pretraining can place the measurement component that harms transfer in known coordinates, so that deployment drops them with a fixed projection and no target data. GlucoPRISM supervises a GlucoFM backbone with response contracts, rules for how each part of the representation should change when only the day or only the sensor changes: a 64-dimensional Trait band should change with neither, a 48-dimensional State band only across days, and a 16-dimensional Sensor band should track the device. Synthetic sensor views calibrated on paired Dexcom and Libre recordings, different-day pairs and glucose-summary targets supply this supervision without clinical labels. Across twelve cross-cohort directions, dropping the Sensor band from the same frozen encoder raises mean transfer AUROC from 68.75 to 73.57, against 69.3 for GlucoFM. The gain has two parts. Into CGMacros, the one target cohort recorded with two sensor types, filtering adds 11 to 19 points, and this holds when the generator is recalibrated on half of the participants and scored on the other half. On the other eight directions filtering is neutral and the encoder itself exceeds GlucoFM by 3.5 points. The device remains linearly decodable after filtering, so the filter removes a device-related component that harms transfer rather than all measurement information. The retained bands improve window AUROC on thirteen of fourteen public task--cohort cells (Holm-adjusted p=0.031) and correlation on fourteen of fifteen clinical endpoints in an external cohort of 9,303 participants.

title: Exploiting Gradients in Bayesian Inference of Expensive Simulators
abstract: Simulators based on differential equations are ubiquitous in science and engineering. They are often used in simulation-based inference to evaluate the posterior distribution of the input parameters based on real-world observations of the simulator outputs. However, inference becomes challenging when individual simulator evaluations are computationally expensive. In such cases, a Bayesian optimization-based active learning approach with Gaussian process surrogate models has been used to maximize the information obtained from a limited simulation budget. Recently, gradients of simulator outputs with respect to input parameters have become increasingly available, yet they are rarely exploited for inference. Even though we only need to learn the simulator input-output relationship, gradient information can provide an additional valuable signal to guide the active learning procedure. This is of particular interest in the case of expensive simulators, when sample efficiency is crucial. In this paper, we demonstrate how incorporating gradient information into the Gaussian process surrogate accelerates Bayesian optimization-based inference under a limited simulation budget. Our results show significant improvement in convergence speed from using gradient information. For reverse-mode differentiation, the inference efficiency gains are maintained when accounting for the additional computational cost. In contrast, for forward-mode differentiation, the inference speed-up does not outweigh the computational costs. These results indicate that gradient-enhanced surrogates are beneficial primarily in problems where the number of parameters exceeds the output dimensionality, where reverse-mode differentiation is efficient.

title: Anytime-valid detection of LLM weight exfiltration
abstract: A compromised LLM inference server can leak model weights by encoding payload bits in otherwise plausible token choices. A replay of the same prompt in a trusted server can expose such deviations, but benign numerical nondeterminism also causes token mismatches. Patient attackers can therefore hide within normal variation unless evidence is combined across responses. We introduce a prompt-level e-process that calibrates whole-response mismatch events on trusted benign traffic and accumulates evidence sequentially while, under a calibration-transfer assumption, controlling the probability of any false alarm over an unbounded monitoring horizon. We evaluate it on four models against a seed-blind attack and a stronger seed-aware attack that hides payload bits only in near-ties to remain stealthy, analyzing the channel capacity vs detectability trade-off. Compared with a hard per-token alarm, the e-process combines weak evidence across responses while providing explicit anytime false-alarm control.

title: TokenBank: Financial Infrastructure for AI Services
abstract: AI services incur inference costs during execution, while revenue may arrive later. Changing API prices, limited upfront capital, and service failures can limit operators' ability to sustain or expand their services. Beyond reducing per-request costs, operators need to plan future spending, fund execution before revenue arrives, and obtain compensation for specified losses. This requires clear agreements across services with different pricing and execution conditions. These agreements must distinguish rights to consume services from rights to receive payments, define obligations under uncertain costs and income, and specify which failures qualify for compensation and how much can be paid. We present TokenBank, a financial infrastructure that represents these commitments through structured contracts. It supports service-consumption rights, agreements that settle API-price differences in cash (forwards), financing through limited rights to future service revenue, and protection claims for specified service failures. Contracts specify participants, covered services, validity, ownership, fulfillment conditions, and settlement rules. Evaluation combines replay of 899,441 API requests, real model-driven agent execution, and contract API tests. In a zero-discount rising-price resampling scenario, forwards reduce mean expenditure by USD 304.88 but increase its standard deviation from USD 1,152.45 to USD 1,190.82. A controlled replication with five portfolios per capital condition finds mean contribution differences between financing and self-funding of +1.0635, -0.1406, and -0.2962 experimental USD under low, baseline, and ample capital, respectively. The evaluation distinguishes contract correctness from economic effectiveness under declared economic and failure assumptions; supplier invoices and commercial revenue are unavailable.

title: QUILT: Rethinking Sparse-Attention Prefill through Shared Query Execution
abstract: Sparse attention reduces the cost of long-context attention, but existing kernels typically process queries independently, repeatedly loading and dequantizing KV entries shared across queries. We observe substantial overlap in the KV entries selected by neighboring queries, creating opportunities for cross-query reuse. We present QUILT, a workload-aware sparse-attention execution mechanism that jointly processes neighboring queries and reuses shared KV entries to reduce redundant memory traffic and computation. QUILT introduces Shift-and-Compare Set Decomposition (SCSD), which transforms irregular set operations into regular data-parallel primitives suitable for modern accelerators, and pipelines SCSD with attention computation to hide its overhead. Cascaded sharing captures reuse hierarchically at multiple granularities. A tile-aware execution strategy balances sharing granularity with hardware tile utilization and selectively removes low-importance query-specific tails to eliminate underutilized tiles. We evaluate QUILT on LongBench using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-3.2 under both tensor and sequence parallelism. Compared with the state-of-the-art sparse-attention kernel, QUILT reduces average kernel latency by up to 55.1% and processed KV data by up to 55.9%, while reducing time-to-first-token (TTFT) latency by up to 36.8% with negligible accuracy degradation.

title: Declarative Dialog Flows for Multi-Tenant Conversational Agents: Design Lessons from ARC
abstract: ARC is a multi-tenant platform on which small businesses build conversational agents for chat, messaging and telephone. Authors draw an agent as a typed node graph covering conversation, logic, data handling and external capabilities, and a server-side runtime executes it together with intent classification, document retrieval and a catalogue of more than 200 integration connectors. This report describes three design choices and the problems that motivated them. First, the flow runtime is a pure step function that advances one user turn and expresses every side effect as an explicit request, so the same graph runs identically in an authoring simulator and in production. Second, agents installed from a shared template now follow that template automatically, using a content-hash version and a conditional write so an upgrade happens exactly once and preserves each business's own integration choices. Third, the variables that automations pass into conversations are governed by one declaration registry checked by a parity test, after the same declaration drift recurred three times and once caused an agent to speak template syntax to a caller. We report the operational measurements we have and state what remains unvalidated.

title: Auditing unsupported claims in LLM-written intrusion alert explanations
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now used to explain intrusion-detection alerts, yet an explanation can sound confident while stating things the evidence does not support. We divide such statements into two tiers. Tier 1 covers unsupported specifics and Tier 2 covers background knowledge that is absent from the evidence, so a single annotation yields both a strict and a lenient policy. We apply a frozen, versioned rule engine to 398 explanations that a Gemini model wrote from six flow features of CIC-IDS 2017 and nothing else; nine features were intended, but three were missing from the alert records of the earlier run. Under the strict policy, 92.5% of explanations (95% CI 89.7–95.0) contain at least one flagged sentence, and under the lenient policy 53.5% (48.5–58.3) do. Of 177 stated flow durations, 176 contradict the documented microsecond unit. At the sentence level, explanations of attack flows are flagged more often than those of normal flows (strict 24.3% vs 17.6%). In an audit of 25 explanations labelled by two AI annotators and adjudicated by the author (inter-annotator kappa 0.83), the rules never flag a sentence that the labels call grounded. They find, however, only 35% of the sentences the labels call unsupported (recall 0.35, 95% CI 0.28–0.44). We also report how an earlier version of this pipeline failed a reproduction, as several of its reported figures could not be recomputed from the saved files. The corpus comes from an earlier, uncontrolled run, the audit is small, and the labels are not an independent human gold standard. A controlled run has been specified but not executed.

title: retestR: Model-Based Anomaly Detection for Repeat Test-Takers
abstract: Model-Based Anomaly Detection for Repeat Test-Takers Version 0.1.0Description Flags repeat test-takers whose second-attempt performance departs from what a growth model predicts, using independent evidence sources: model-expected score gain (accounting for regression to the mean, time between attempts and remediation), differential performance on exposed versus new items (Sinharay, 2017, ),and differential response speed under a lognormal response-time model (van der Linden, 2006, ). Evidence is combined into a risk index calibrated by parametric bootstrap under the no-misconduct model, so flagging thresholds carry explicit false-positive rates.

title: A novel privacy-preserving large language model integrating trust-weighted and ethical gradient masking
abstract: Large language models face a critical privacy utility tradeoff because training data contains personally identifiable information vulnerable to extraction attacks, while existing differential privacy methods significantly degrade model performance. This work proposes the trust-weighted and ethical gradient model, a novel privacy-preserving model that addresses challenges through three integrated mechanisms. First, trust-weighted memory employs per-sample weighting based on data sensitivity to reduce memorization of sensitive information while preserving learning signals from non-sensitive data. Second, ethical gradient masking combines per-sample clipping and Gaussian noise with sensitivity-based soft masking under a tracked ( ϵ , δ ) privacy budget, while maintaining utility. Third, the ethical boundary layer classifies and mitigates risky outputs before delivery, providing a final defense against privacy leakage. A distinctive feature of the proposed approach is the integration of computational interpretations of trustworthiness, privacy, and non-intrusion into artificial intelligence privacy systems. Extensive experiments on the Pile dataset demonstrate that trust-weighted and ethical gradient models achieve a reduction in personally identifiable information leakage while maintaining baseline utility, outperforming baseline differential privacy methods in this evaluation. The model exhibits strong resistance against membership inference, extraction attacks, and linkage attacks for privacy-preserving large language model training. The selective masking improves utility compared to uniform differential privacy under the same privacy budget.

title: How Do Hardware Faults Manifest Differently in LLM Agents?
abstract: We present the first systematic study of the resilience of large language model (LLM) agents to random hardware-induced faults. Prior work on hardware fault resilience in LLMs focuses on model-level outcomes, such as incorrect outputs or generation failures. Yet LLM agents repeatedly interact with tools and environments, creating loops that can change how hardware faults manifest. We conduct an extensive evaluation across three agent benchmarks, comprising 6,814 agent executions: 2,400+ clean runs and 4,300+ fault-injected runs with independently sampled random two-bit weight faults. We trace how these faults propagate through agent execution. Unlike prior studies, we find that agentic execution transforms model-level corruption into distinct system-level outcomes: (1) agents can recover from faulty model outputs and still complete tasks correctly; (2) this recovery increases computational and execution costs; (3) a few faults cause subtle but semantically meaningful errors while the agent otherwise behaves normally; and (4) for some models and scenarios, faults can alter security and alignment behavior.

title: A Minimal Optical-Flow Representation for Vision-Based Tactile Rotation Classification in Robotic Manipulation Across Gravity Domains
abstract: Vision-based tactile sensors provide rich contact information, but processing high-resolution images can be costly for resource-constrained platforms such as space robots. This work investigates whether a compact representation of tactile motion can classify object rotation across different gravity conditions. Dense optical flow from a simulated GelSight Mini is aggregated over a 7x9 grid into 126 features and used to classify the direction of load-induced rotation under Earth, Mars, Moon, and orbital gravity. Gravity causes a small but significant shift in these features, accounting for 1.6% of their variance (R2 = 0.016). Despite its small magnitude, this shift affects models trained only on Earth data: XGBoost accuracy decreases from 94.4% on Earth to 75.9% in orbit. In contrast, a single model trained across all four gravity domains achieves 96.3% overall accuracy and 95.1%-97.0% across individual domains, without using gravity as an input. The representation can also be reduced to 40 features while retaining 95.7% accuracy, with XGBoost requiring only 0.14 ms per inference. evidence.abstract: Vision-based tactile sensors provide rich contact information, but processing high-resolution images can be costly for resource-constrained platforms such as space robots. This work investigates whether a compact representation of tactile motion can classify object rotation across different gravity conditions. Dense optical flow from a simulated GelSight Mini is aggregated over a 7x9 grid into 126 features and used to classify the direction of load-induced rotation under Earth, Mars, Moon, and orbital gravity. Gravity causes a small but significant shift in these features, accounting for 1.6% of their variance (R2 = 0.016). Despite its small magnitude, this shift affects models trained only on Earth data: XGBoost accuracy decreases from 94.4% on Earth to 75.9% in orbit. In contrast, a single model trained across all four gravity domains achieves 96.3% overall accuracy and 95.1%-97.0% across individual domains, without using gravity as an input. The representation can also be reduced to 40 features while retaining 95.7% accuracy, with XGBoost requiring only 0.14 ms per inference. title: Local Sensitivity in Exponential Selection: Failure Modes and Valid Calibrations
abstract: Selection is a task that chooses one element from a finite public candidate range to maximize a data-dependent score. In differential privacy (DP), the exponential mechanism (EM) samples a candidate at a temperature calibrated to the global sensitivity. In this paper, we study when dataset-dependent sensitivity can safely replace global sensitivity in private selection. We propose three valid approaches. First, a private, high-probability upper bound on local sensitivity yields approximate DP, and the method extends to finite higher-order sensitivity hierarchies. Second, our Propose-Test-Release (PTR) variant privately searches a finite public grid for a temperature scale rather than fixing it in advance. Third, smooth sensitivity supports several designs. A candidate-independent smooth geometric construction produces a sensitivity envelope that is admissible under the local dampening framework, which privacy is guaranteed for any admissible envelope. Additionally, a separate logarithmic transformation utilizes smooth sensitivity to produce a smoothed candidate score function with advantages: having controlled global sensitivity, and preserving the maximizers of the original utility score, i.e., candidates maximizing the utility. Both of the designs yield range-independent pure DP. Besides that, we also give two approximate DP private selectors using smooth sensitivity: a direct EM with smooth sensitivity calibrated to the candidate range and privacy parameters that matches a theoretical lower bound up to some constant factor, and one using a privatized smooth upper scale by analyzing the logarithmic transform of the smoothness. For every proposed mechanism, we derive a high-probability regret bound under its stated conditions.

title: From Video Clips to Creation Trajectory: Sora100K for AI-Native Video Creation
abstract: AI-Native video creation is shifting from isolated video clips toward iterative video creation workflows. However, existing datasets remain largely video clips, representing video generation and editing as separate tasks rather than connected stages of a video creation workflow. In this paper, we introduce Sora100K, a dataset that represents the AI-Native video creation workflow as a structured video creation trajectory. Specifically, we first identify video creation trajectories and decompose them into three subsets according to their structural roles: text-to-video generation records as roots, single-turn video editing records as editing edges, and multi-turn video editing records as complete trajectories. Then, we use a VLM to assign semantic annotations for generation roots and editing-operation annotations for editing edges. A strict construction pipeline further reconstructs source-to-edit lineage, editing order, and intermediate video states while ensuring data quality. Finally, we perform lightweight adaptation on LTX-2 models to assess the supervision value of Sora100K. The results show improvements in visual quality, multi-shot generation, and cross-shot consistency, while successive-turn evaluation reveals that following multi-turn editing instructions remains challenging. Sora100K establishes a new data foundation for AI-Native video creation beyond isolated video clips and toward structured video creation trajectory. The dataset and supplementary materials are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ysicong/Sora100K.

title: Conditional Transfer from Controlled Pretraining Mixtures to Code
abstract: Synthetic tasks are increasingly used both as probes of language-model capability and as pretraining data. Both uses are often justified by loss reduction: falling loss is treated as informative, and faster loss reduction with more sampling as evidence that a task is worth sampling. We separate three signals. A task is diagnostic when its loss tracks global pretraining progress; it is teachable when its loss responds to its own token budget; and a data source transfers when including it improves a downstream target. We study controlled pretraining in which 70% of the corpus is fixed general Python and the remaining 30% is a simplex over three source families: OpenCodeInstruct, a curated suite of 12 code-adjacent synthetic tasks, and 15 literature-derived probe tasks. Across a task-budget sweep we detect teachability for 14 of 27 tasks, with a sharp asymmetry between the two synthetic families (10/12 curated versus 4/15 literature-derived). Teachability and downstream transfer give different rankings. On the mixture-simplex edge between the curated suite and OpenCodeInstruct, HumanEval pass@20 after a fixed fine-tuning stage rises from 15.9 at pure curated data to its highest observed value, 22.6, at a mixture that is 75% OpenCodeInstruct, then falls to 19.5 at pure OpenCodeInstruct. Curated synthetic data therefore has conditional value: it contributes as a limited share of a mixture that a target-aligned source still dominates. Finally, a loss-based adaptive scheduler exposes the mismatch between residual loss reducibility and downstream transfer. Across three 60k-step free-ratio runs, Ado drives the OpenCodeInstruct share below 5% within the first 5k steps and to 1.2--1.4% by the end of training, and underperforms its matched fixed-mixture controls by 2.4--11.0 percentage points. Optimizing near-term task-loss reduction moves the mixture away from the region that transfers.

title: ReCal: Calibrating Structured Pruning for On-Policy Distillation Recovery
abstract: Structured pruning reduces the deployment cost of reasoning language models, but the resulting capability degradation can hinder subsequent on-policy distillation (OPD) recovery. Because OPD relies on student-generated trajectories, pruning damage that persists after offline distillation can limit its effectiveness. We propose RECAL, Recovery-Aware Calibration, a simple plug-and-play approach that improves OPD recovery by adjusting calibration before pruning. RECAL uses forward KL between an unpruned teacher and a pruned probe to identify teacher-supported predictions disrupted by pruning, then reweights calibration statistics to guide existing pruning criteria toward preserving these predictions. Across multiple models and pruning methods, RECAL consistently improves mathematical reasoning after OPD, achieving gains of up to 16.7 percentage points on AIME, alongside improvements in most code-generation comparisons. Further analysis shows that RECAL reduces residual damage at heavily affected tokens and establishes performance advantages that persist through recovery. These results demonstrate the value of recovery-aware calibration for improving on-policy distillation recovery of pruned reasoning models.

title: Machine Learning Optimization for Enhanced OS Fingerprinting
abstract: Operating System (OS) Fingerprinting is a technique that can be used to identify a network's operating systems by evaluating network traffic in the form of TCP/IP packets. This research will explore the effectiveness of passively identifying operating systems on the CIC-IDS2017 dataset, a collection of over 47 gigabytes of pcap files with their corresponding operating systems. This research also proposes a new command line interface, OsirisML, which uses nPrint to preprocess the data into tabular data and XGBoost to apply ML to the data to generate, retrain, and test ML models. When packets are split randomly between training and testing, OsirisML models reach an accuracy of 97.66% on a down-sampled subset of the Friday capture and 84.69% on the entire capture. On the entire Monday capture, which contains no attacks, OsirisML reaches an accuracy of 73.83% and an F-1 score of 79.38%.

title: Enhancing Privacy and Collaborative Efforts in Healthcare through Federated Machine Learning
abstract: Healthcare institutions create data from complementary electronic health records, medical images, laboratory measurements, genomic profiles, and connected devices. While aggregating this data can enhance machine-learning models, centralized collection increases exposure risks, conflicts with institutional data sovereignty, and is often constrained by legal, ethical, and operational challenges. Federated Machine Learning (FML) provides a collaborative framework where participating organizations can train a common model while keeping raw data stored locally. This paper presents a design-oriented review and a practical framework for privacy-aware, cross-silo FML in healthcare. The framework integrates local data governance, standardized preprocessing, federated optimization, secure aggregation, differential privacy, update validation, audit logging, and continuous clinical monitoring. It explicitly distinguishes data locality from formal privacy guarantees: while federated training minimizes raw data movement, model updates can still leak information or be subject to manipulation. An illustrative experiment involving five statistically heterogeneous synthetic hospitals evaluated centralized learning, isolated local learning, federated averaging, and clipped-and-noised federated averaging. The results indicate that beneficial collaboration is technically feasible, but privacy, fairness, interoperability, governance, and clinical validation must be engineered as integral parts of the joint lifecycle requirements rather than treated as consequences of federation alone.

title: NULL-SPACING PREPROCESSING FOR UAV CLASSIFICATION FROM RF IQ SIGNALS UNDER ISM-BAND INTERFERENCE
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) classification from radio-frequency (RF) in-phase/quadrature (IQ) signals in industrial, scientific, and medical (ISM) bands is often degraded by background noise and co-channel interference. This paper investigates Null-Spacing as an IQ-domain preprocessing step that attenuates structured interference before short-time Fourier transform (STFT) or continuous wavelet transform (CWT) representation. The interference subspace is estimated from Wi-Fi/Bluetooth samples in the training set, and each IQ signal is projected onto its orthogonal complement. The method is evaluated on the CardRF dataset with five UAV classes under additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mixed interference, and jointly negative signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and signal-to-interference ratio (SIR) conditions. With the STFT + convolutional neural network (CNN) configuration at η = 0.99, Null-Spacing improves macro-F1 from 82.82% to 84.56% and accuracy from 82.95% to 84.61%. Under negative-SNR AWGN, macro-F1 increases by 9.165 percentage points. Control experiments further show that the gain does not come from arbitrary projection alone, but from an interference subspace derived from Wi-Fi/Bluetooth references. The results support Null-Spacing as a conditional preprocessing step: it improves robustness under several difficult noisy and interfered conditions, but is not uniformly beneficial across all signal conditions

title: Predictive Guest Experience Engineering in Hospitality 5.0 by Integrating AI, IoT Analytics, and Behavioral Data for Hyper Personalized Services
abstract: This chapter focuses on how artificial intelligence, IoT Analytics, and Behavioral Data Science can be used in the Hospitality 5.0 model for achieving personalized guest experience. As part of this effort, the Predictive Guest Experience Engineering (PGEE) approach relies on various sources of hospitality data ranging from guest booking behavior, IoT sensors in hotel rooms, guest mobile application usage, to guest reviews to create predictive models that can anticipate guest behavior. The chapter will make use of Hotel Reviews and Guest Behavior data set and employ exploratory data analysis techniques along with statistical hypothesis testing methods, and supervised machine learning models such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, XGBoost, and Multi-layered Neural Network. XGBoost yields the best accuracy rate of 92.7%, with AUC-ROC at 0.968, proving its effectiveness as the most efficient predictive model in the PGEE system. In this chapter, the PGEE system is introduced as an innovative concept, combining behavioral segmentation, predictive modeling, and personalization.

title: Review of: "From Informal to Formal – Incorporating and Evaluating LLMs on Natural Language Requirements to Verifiable Formal Proofs"
abstract: What the work claimsThe paper starts from the observation that end-to-end benchmarks mix problem-solving, reasoning, and the writing of formal speci cations.To separate these skills, the authors split the path from an informal requirement to a veri able proof into six tasks: requirement analysis (ReqAna), full proof generation (ProofGen), proof segment generation (SegGen), proof completion (ProofComplete), proof in lling (ProofIn ll), and proof generation from code (Code2Proof) (Section 2, Figure 2).Five formal languages are covered: Coq, Lean4, Dafny, ACSL, and TLA+ (Section 3.1).Proofs were collected from open-source GitHub repositories and kept only if they verify.They were then split into segments and described in natural language by a GPT-4 family model (Section 3.2; the Abstract names gpt-4o).This gives about 18k instruction-response pairs, divided 8:2 into the ne-tuning set FM-ALPACA (14k) and the benchmark FM-BENCH (about 4k) (Section 3.3, Tables 1 and 2).Formal outputs are scored by running the real veri ers: the Coq, Lean4, and Dafny environments, TLC for TLA+, and Frama-C for ACSL.ReqAna is scored by BLEU (Section 3.4).Ten open models are evaluated without ne-tuning, and three base models of 7B to 8B are ne-tuned (Section 4.1).The authors report that, without ne-tuning, the models do best on Code2Proof, with an average Pass@1 of 43.57%.They do worst on ProofGen (8.65%) and SegGen (10.61%) (Section 4.2).For SegGen, ACSL is the easiest language (average 34.92%), followed by Dafny (15.97%) (Section 4.3).Fine-tuning on FM-ALPACA lifts the 7B to 8B models to the level of DeepSeek-R1 (27.31% against 27.11%) (Section 4.4).Fine-tuning on Qeios qeios.

title: Adaptive kernel learning using genetic programming in reproducing kernel banach spaces
abstract: Constructing effective kernel functions remains a fundamental problem in kernel-based machine learning. Most existing approaches are developed within Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (RKHS), where the feature-space geometry is fixed and may limit flexibility in representing complex data distributions. This paper presents Evo-RK, an evolutionary framework for automatically constructing semi-inner product reproducing kernels in Reproducing Kernel Banach Spaces (RKBS). The proposed framework employs genetic programming (GP) to jointly evolve nonlinear feature mappings and the Banach space geometric parameter ( p ), while guaranteeing kernel validity through an explicit embedding in the ℓ p sequence space. This formulation allows the feature-space geometry to adapt to the learning task during kernel evolution. Experiments on six benchmark datasets, including UCI tabular datasets and MedMNIST medical image datasets, demonstrate the effectiveness of Evo-RK for both support vector machine (SVM) classification and kernel principal component analysis (KPCA). Compared with a genetic-programming-based Hilbert-space kernel baseline, Evo-RK matches or improves classification accuracy while consistently producing sparser decision functions. Further analysis shows that the evolved kernels naturally exhibit hierarchical compositions and task-dependent geometric adaptation, with quasi-Hilbert geometries preferred for classification tasks and stronger geometric deformation emerging in unsupervised feature extraction. These results demonstrate that jointly evolving kernel representations and Banach space geometry provides an effective approach for constructing task-adaptive kernels while improving model sparsity.

title: Data-driven Optimal Sensor Placement for Aerosol Monitoring in the UK
abstract: We develop a data-driven sensor-placement framework and apply it to aerosol monitoring in the United Kingdom (UK). A trained convolutional Gaussian neural process is embedded within the DeepSensor optimisation framework. Genetic optimisation with lazy evaluation and caching reduces mean computational time by 60\% (10$\pm$3 versus 25$\pm$7 minutes) while producing sequential placement performance comparable to the greedy solver. Using the CAMS reference field to construct a retrospective oracle benchmark, Joint NLL improves by about 22\% for Joint-MI-driven genetic placement after five locations for aerosol stations are identified. Seasonal and wind-regime analyses show that agreement between model-based criteria and oracle benchmarks varies with meteorological transport conditions. These results show a computationally efficient approach for data-informed expansion of environmental observing systems.

title: Optimal linear-optical interferometers for unitary t-designs in a multi-photon Fock space
abstract: We investigate the construction of unitary $t$-designs in a multi-photon Fock space on programmable linear-optical interferometers. Using the frame potential as the optimization objective, we identify architectures that realize approximate unitary 1- and 2-designs with considerably fewer controllable parameters than required for universal linear optics. For example, we find numerical evidence suggesting that for unitary 1-designs, the required number of programmable parameters scales empirically as $2d$ with the number of modes $d$, instead of $O(d^2)$. We benchmark the resulting ensembles using single-photon transition probabilities and average channel fidelities. Furthermore, as a practical result, we develop a photon-number estimation protocol for multi-photon Fock states that leverages these optimized 1- and 2-designs. Our findings demonstrate that shallow interferometers can accurately reproduce Haar-averaged first moments, while second-moment-sensitive observables provide a considerably stricter test for approximate unitary 2-designs.

title: Enriched Holomorphic Neural Networks for 2D and 3D Laplace Problems
abstract: Boundary-value problems for the Laplace equation develop singular behaviour near corners, edges and junctions that smooth approximators resolve poorly. We combine holomorphic neural networks with singular functions derived from the local geometry and boundary conditions. The representation is harmonic by construction, so no interior residual is needed: the network fits the smooth remainder from boundary data alone, and the enrichment terms capture the singular behaviour. Singular exponents are trainable, so the construction also applies when the local expansion is not known in advance. We extend the approach to three dimensions using independent networks evaluated along complex null directions. The enriched model is the most accurate tested method on every problem. Its margin is several orders of magnitude where the enrichment captures the singularity exactly, and a factor of about 1.7-2.1 over the next-best method on a CdZnTe radiation detector with many singular sites, in both two and three dimensions.

title: Asymptotic Safety in Gauge Theories beyond Four Dimensions: Perturbative Tests and Fixed-Point Mergers
abstract: Non-Abelian gauge theories above four dimensions may admit an interacting ultraviolet fixed point through the competition between canonical scaling and gauge-field antiscreening. Using the four-loop mathrm{MS} beta function continued to D=4+2ε, we determine the largest dimension D_{pt}=4+2ε_{pt} below which successive loop corrections to the fixed point remain hierarchically ordered under a specified ratio criterion, and map D_{pt} over color and flavor numbers for fermions in the fundamental representation of SU(N). At D=5, we construct rational anomalous dimensions with a fixed, pole-regularized denominator inspired by the functional renormalization group (fRG). Matching to the mathrm{MS} series through one, two, and three loops produces progressively smaller shifts in the critical flavor number and coupling at the ultraviolet--infrared merger (the point where the infrared and ultraviolet fixed points coincide), yielding N_f^{cr}simeq 2.09 , N at large N in the three-loop construction. This low-order stabilization, together with qualitative evidence from fRG flows including higher gauge operators, suggests a potential merger scenario that bounds the candidate asymptotically safe region in flavor number. The resulting color--flavor map provides guidance for five-dimensional model building by displaying both the baseline perturbative-control boundary and the candidate three-loop merger boundary. Four-loop matching, however, retains an interacting ultraviolet fixed point beyond the three-loop merger boundary, with no merger found for integer 2le Nle15 and 0le N_f/Nle11/2. The sensitivity of the fixed-point structure to higher-order terms leaves both scenarios open, highlighting fixed-point annihilation as a potential constraint on five-dimensional asymptotic safety.

title: OX-NeRF: 3D X-ray Tomography Reconstruction from Sparse Views Using Implicit Neural Representation
abstract: NeRF and Gaussian splatting methods have been successfully applied on X-ray scenes where the views are too sparse for 3D reconstruction via classical methods. Ultra-sparse scenes with 10 or fewer views such as those with high-rate or low-dose acquisition still, however, present a significant challenge. To address this problem we present a new framework, Optimised X-ray Neural Radiance Fields (OX-NeRF), that combines cross-scene feature learning with scene-specific optimisation to reconstruct sets of related scenes. OX-NeRF employs a convolutional neural network (CNN) to identify cross-scene features while maintaining scene-specific multi-resolution hash grids of spatial features. The paired representations are fused and passed to a multilayer perceptron (MLP); the CNN, hash grids and MLP are then jointly optimised end-to-end. Benchmarking on parallel-beam and cone-beam X-ray datasets shows OX-NeRF provides significantly higher reconstruction accuracy on ultra-sparse scenes compared to existing radiance field methods.

title: Should Your Database Systems Use Hardware-Assisted Memory Safety Extensions in Production?
abstract: Database systems are predominantly developed in unsafe languages (e.g., C/C++) to meet performance requirements through low-level memory management, yet this reliance renders them prone to systemic memory-safety issues that compromise reliability, consistency, security, and durability. Through an extensive bug analysis of prominent database systems, we show that these memory-safety issues persist in production environments despite advancements in database testing tools. While emerging hardware-assisted extensions, such as Arm's Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) and CHERI, offer a promising mitigation path for memory safety, their practical applicability and performance overhead within the specialized constraints of database systems remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we evaluate hardware extensions through the lens of what we define as the database trilemma: the fundamental trade-off between safety, performance, and portability, to determine their viability for production-grade database systems. We provide the first side-by-side comparison of MTE and CHERI across a database workload suite. Our bottom-up study spans microarchitecture, the compiler/runtime/OS stack, core data structures (ART, B+Tree, hash table, skip list, linked list, and queue), and full database systems (Redis, LevelDB, SQLite, MySQL, DuckDB, and LadyBugDB) to characterize their performance, safety guarantees, and ease of adoption. We find that while hardware extensions can offer near-deterministic protection, they introduce non-uniform performance taxes: MTE provides high portability with modest overheads (~10%), while CHERI delivers superior safety guarantees with higher performance penalties (20-60%) and significant porting effort. Our study equips database systems architects with an actionable guide toward building the next generation of reliable, secure databases using hardware-assisted safety mechanisms.

title: Photon evolution through light-particle conversion in stochastic magnetic fields: Kramers--Kronig relations and universality
abstract: We study photon conversion into light particles, such as dilatons, axions, and gravitons, induced by background magnetic fields, and formulate the resulting evolution in terms of the Stokes parameters. We show that photon conversion reduces to an effective non-unitary evolution of the photon sector. In the perturbative regime, the Hermitian and anti-Hermitian parts of the effective photon Hamiltonian are related through Kramers--Kronig relations, revealing that the changes in the Stokes parameters are not independent. We apply this general framework to photon evolution in Gaussian stochastic magnetic fields with possible helicity, and derive the ensemble-averaged evolution of the Stokes parameters. We find that two nonzero contributions arise even in the absence of magnetic helicity, which respectively correspond to the overall attenuation of all the Stokes parameters and to an irrelevant overall phase. We also find that magnetic helicity gives rise to two additional contributions, one of which changes the circular polarization while the other induces a rotation of linear polarization. These contributions form two Kramers--Kronig pairs. In particular, photon conversion induced by magnetic helicity is accompanied by both circular-polarization and birefringent responses. The same structure appears in dilaton-photon, axion-photon, and graviton-photon systems, revealing universality of photon conversion in magnetic fields.

title: Human–AI Collaboration in Digital Marketing: Evidence from an Emerging Economy, Somalia
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping digital marketing through automation, customer analytics, personalization, and data-driven decision-making. However, empirical evidence on human–AI collaboration in emerging and fragile economies remains limited. This study examined the adoption of human–AI collaboration in digital marketing among businesses in Somalia, identified key barriers to AI adoption, and assessed the association between human–AI collaboration and customer engagement, marketing efficiency, and business growth. The study used a positivist research approach and a quantitative cross-sectional survey design. Data were collected from 86 business owners, marketing managers, digital marketing specialists, and ICT/technology officers using purposive sampling. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Spearman's rank correlation, and multiple linear regression. Respondents reported frequent use of AI-assisted content creation, customer analytics, marketing automation, social media management, and AI-supported decision-making. The principal barriers were limited technical skills, limited infrastructure, implementation costs, data privacy concerns, and organizational resistance to change. Spearman's correlations indicated positive associations between human–AI collaboration and customer engagement (ρ = .684), marketing efficiency (ρ =.725), and business growth (ρ = .658), all reported at p < .001. Regression models explained 50.7% of the variance in customer engagement, 54.9% in marketing efficiency, and 46.4% in business growth. Human–AI collaboration was positively associated with each outcome after controlling for organizational size and industry sector. Because the study is cross-sectional and based on a purposive sample, the findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. The results highlight the importance of combining AI capabilities with human judgment, creativity, contextual knowledge, and responsible data practices in Somalia's digital marketing environment.

title: Polar Fox Optimization Algorithm for the Multiple Sequence Alignment
abstract: Overview This repository contains the standalone Python implementation of the Polar Fox Optimization (PFA) algorithm adapted specifically for the discrete, NP-hard problem of Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA). The script implements a specialized discrete metaheuristic framework that maps continuous swarm intelligence dynamics into discrete biological sequence spaces. By combining a heterogeneous multi-clan population architecture with domain-specific sequence manipulation operators, the algorithm optimizes alignment topologies using the BLOSUM62 substitution matrix and affine gap penalties. Key Algorithmic Features Discrete Sequence Mapping & Initialization: Converts variable-length biological sequences into valid candidate alignment matrices using random gap-insertion strategies while strictly preserving sequence integrity. Heterogeneous Multi-Clan Skulk Architecture: Group A (Explorers): High-capacity gap perturbation (up to 50 gap shifts per cycle) dedicated to global topology exploration and escaping deep local gap traps. Group B (Exploiters): Fine-grained local refinement (5 gap mutations per cycle) for optimizing localized alignment blocks. Group C & D (Balanced & Conservative): Intermediate search intensity and conservative structural preservation of candidate alignments. Specialized Discrete Movement Operators: Two-Point Sequence Fragmentation Crossover: Leader-guided crossover phase broadcasting structural breakthrough alignments across the skulk. BLOSUM62-Guided Fitness Function: Objective evaluation function rewarding evolutionary amino acid conservation and penalizing gap openings and extensions. Self-Contained & Configurable: Fully configurable execution parameters including population size, generation limits, evaluation budgets (NFE), gap penalties, and mutation probabilities. System Requirements & Dependencies Language: Python 3.8+ Core Libraries: numpy, pandas

title: Theory of Everything Research Programme: Block III Retention, Feedback and Learning Confirmatory Dataset and Decision Record.
abstract: This dataset release provides the original confirmatory evidence and preregistered decision record for Experimental Block III of the Theory of Everything Research Programme. The study was preregistered at OSF under DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/8ZWM7 before any held-out confirmatory seed was executed. The release contains seven provenance-valid confirmatory raw study trees generated from twenty held-out seeds, including trajectory records, retained-state interventions, feedback-channel perturbations, learning-update controls, full factorial R × F × L records, seed registries, provenance metadata, processed metrics, figures and decision records. The preregistered decisions were RETAIN for H3.1 through H3.7. Retention was selectively useful when relevant history was unavailable from the present observable state and targeted retained-state interventions predictably altered behaviour. Closed-loop feedback was selectively useful under unpredictable disturbance and degraded systematically under delays and channel corruption. Between-episode learning selectively adapted to changed mappings and persisted after parameter updates were frozen. The full factorial study retained mechanism separability. The release also preserves the serious bypass results. Direct present-state augmentation reproduced the relevant historical information without online retained state; matched open-loop control was sufficient in predictable disturbance; and explicit contextual mapping information produced successful behaviour without parameter learning. These bypasses limit claims of universal necessity while leaving the registered causal-use results intact. All seven confirmatory runs completed once with provenance PASS. Independent analysis regeneration reproduced all substantive tables, the figure and the human-readable decision summary exactly; the JSON scientific content was identical apart from a fresh creation timestamp. This release is paired with the Block III software and reproducibility package (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23244848) and implements the experimental framework described in Working Paper III (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22857230). The results do not establish general intelligence, explicit world modelling, counterfactual planning, reflective self-awareness or phenomenal consciousness.

title: Data Structures by Design: From Computational Questions to Algorithms, Invariants, and Intelligent Systems
abstract: BOOK PREVIEW — Data Structures by Design: From Computational Questions to Algorithms, Invariants, and Intelligent Systems Every data structure answers a question. Every answer has a boundary. Why do two programs storing identical information behave so differently? Why does a representation that works perfectly today become inefficient or unreliable when requirements change? And how can we determine whether a data structure is genuinely appropriate for the problem it is intended to solve? Data Structures by Design approaches these questions by treating data structures as decisions to be understood, tested, and defended—not merely implementations to be memorized. This book preview presents Chapter 1, “What Does It Mean to Organize Information?” Through a recurring university information platform, the chapter introduces computational questions, operations, workloads, logical and physical representations, abstract data types, operation contracts, and representation invariants. Worked examples, algorithms, executable Python code, design challenges, and exercises guide readers from understanding how information is organized to examining why a particular organization succeeds, where its limitations emerge, and when another design becomes necessary. The book develops a question-driven approach to learning data structures, connecting theoretical foundations with algorithmic reasoning, programming, correctness, and practical design decisions. This publication contains Chapter 1 only and is made available as an academic preview of the forthcoming textbook.

title: APPLICATION OF LINEAR OPERATORS AND TENSOR PRODUCTS IN QUANTUM ENTANGLEMENT AND QUANTUM COMPUTING
abstract: Quantum computing is fundamentally based on the mathematical structure of complex Hilbert spaces, linear operators, tensor products, and unitary transformations. Among these concepts, tensor products provide the formal mechanism for constructing the state space of composite quantum systems, whereas linear and unitary operators describe quantum transformations, measurements, and computational gates. This article examines the mathematical relationship between linear operators and tensor products and analyzes their role in the formation, manipulation, and characterization of quantum entanglement. Particular attention is given to two-qubit systems, separable and entangled states, Schmidt decomposition, controlled operations, and the role of non-factorizable operators in quantum circuits. The analysis demonstrates that tensor products perform a dual function: they provide the mathematical representation of composite systems and enable the construction of local operations acting on individual subsystems. At the same time, genuinely entangling transformations, such as the controlled-NOT operation, cannot in general be represented as a single tensor product of independent local operators. Recent research further demonstrates that tensor-product and operator-Schmidt decompositions can be used to characterize operator entanglement, reduce circuit complexity, and construct efficient representations of quantum processes. The results establish that linear algebra and tensor-product structures are not merely formal tools but constitute the mathematical foundation connecting quantum entanglement with quantum computation.

title: Projected Primal–Dual Gradient Preference Optimization Under Category-Wise Split-Conformal Safety Constraints for Large Language Model Post-Training
abstract: Preference optimisation improves helpfulness, but a single aggregate safety penalty lets frequent harm categories dominate the objective while rare ones bear the residual risk. This paper models post-training as a vector-constrained programme: the pairwise preference loss is minimised under one risk tolerance per harm category. The solver is a projected primal–dual gradient recursion that prices each category by its own residual violation. For a nonconvex objective we bound three horizon-averaged residuals—primal stationarity, dual regret and the average constraint value—for the unbiased, unclipped recursion and a uniformly drawn iterate; the implemented recursion is compared empirically with a no-EMA, no-clipping form of itself. Certification stays separate from optimisation: on an untouched calibration split, a multiplicity-adjusted fixed-sequence test gives release thresholds valid for all categories at once under correct category assignment, with an additive bound for learned routers. It certifies the scoring and filtering of corpus-distributed candidate responses, not text the trained policy generates. In one exploratory setting—one Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct backbone, PKU-SafeRLHF, three seeds—the recursion meets the per-category tolerance that direct preference optimisation and scalar-constrained schemes violate, cutting the worst-category miss rate at the training threshold from 0.176 to 0.057 at unchanged preference accuracy. The certified operating point barely moves: most of the constraint’s effect is a score translation shared by the harmful and benign responses of a prompt, which calibration provably absorbs. Whether a training constraint holds and whether the deployed gate is safer are different questions.

In one exploratory setting—one Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct backbone, PKU-SafeRLHF, three seeds—the recursion meets the per-category tolerance that direct preference optimisation and scalar-constrained schemes violate, cutting the worst-category miss rate at the training threshold from 0.176 to 0.057 at unchanged preference accuracy. The certified operating point barely moves: most of the constraint’s effect is a score translation shared by the harmful and benign responses of a prompt, which calibration provably absorbs. Whether a training constraint holds and whether the deployed gate is safer are different questions.

title: Spatiotemporal Multi-Horizon Solar Irradiance Forecasting in High-Potential Microclimates: A Comparative Benchmark from Linear Baselines to Deep Learning and Foundation Models
abstract: The operational integration of solar energy into modern power grids, particularly for day-ahead markets and battery storage scheduling, requires highly accurate, multi-horizon irradiance forecasts to mitigate cloud-induced intermittency. This study evaluates a spatiotemporal, multi-horizon (24-h) Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) forecasting framework across a high-resolution 167-node microclimate in Tula, Tamaulipas, Mexico, using a robust 2020–2024 baseline. We benchmarked six predictive paradigms: diurnal persistence, linear regression, tree ensembles (Extra Trees and XGBoost), a zero-shot foundation model (TimesFM), and a deep CNN–LSTM network, using historical clear-sky irradiance sequences and strictly causal meteorological features. On the independent 2024 test set, XGBoost achieved the lowest macro-average RMSE (120.87Wm−2), but Diebold–Mariano testing confirmed that it was statistically equivalent to the CNN–LSTM architecture. XGBoost showed significant superiority at ultra-short horizons (t+1 and t+2) by efficiently capturing nonlinear radiative inertia, whereas CNN–LSTM minimized errors under sustained overcast regimes and produced the sharpest empirical 95% prediction intervals. At the 24-h mark, ordinary linear regression converged, whereas the complex models did not, highlighting a physical transition toward deterministic solar geometry. Remarkably, zero-shot TimesFM outperformed diurnal persistence without any domain-specific training. Conditional Tree SHAP interpretability demonstrated that the XGBoost model dynamically reallocated predictive weight, shifting from contemporaneous irradiance under clear skies to precipitable water during volatile, intermittent conditions.

title: How does conversation unfold? analyzing learner–LLM dialogues through multiple analytical lenses
abstract: As Large Language Models increasingly permeate educational scenarios, understanding the dynamics of learner-LLM collaboration has become a priority for learning analytics research. Existing approaches, however, tend to rely on surface-level metrics or single perspective coding schemes, limiting insight into the multifaceted nature of these exchanges. This study introduces an analytical framework that combines three theoretically grounded coding schemes with process mining techniques to analyze learner-LLM collaboration in a metacognitive learning task. We applied the framework to 159 conversations from 78 higher education students interacting with a Socratic LLM-based chatbot deployed in a Thermodynamics course, identifying patterns in dialogue structure, epistemic contribution, and conversational balance. For each coding scheme, cluster analysis identified distinct interaction profiles, capturing meaningful variability beneath aggregate patterns. Results reveal that dialogue was structurally dominated by the LLM, yet epistemic contributions were similar in proportion between agents despite pronounced asymmetry in utterance volume. Cross-scheme comparison showed that the three schemes produced related but non-equivalent partitions, each capturing a complementary dimension of the same conversations. Furthermore, learners and the LLM assumed clearly differentiated interactive roles, consistent with a tutor-student dynamic. These findings illustrate the value of multi-perspective, process-oriented frameworks for studying learner-LLM dialogues.

title: A Physics-Informed Hybrid Forward-Inverse Machine Learning Framework for High-Dimensional Sparse Recipe Reconstruction
abstract: High-dimensional sparse recipe formulation in process industries involves nonlinear association of various covariates, bounded by sparsity constraints and multi-criteria tolerances. Traditional physics-based classical methods (such as Kubelka-Munk) fail to generate sparse candidate recipes properly due to their simplified assumptions and industrial process variations. This study proposes a hybrid physics-informed uncertainty-aware framework that is structured into three modules: (a) Module A, a multi-target forward quality model; (b) Module B, a sparse inverse reconstructor; and (c) Module C, a feasibility-constrained ranking layer. Then it has been validated in an industrial textile dyeing context with recipe-grouped cross-validation under multi-illuminant quality assessment comprising process and production information, target reflectance, K/S values, and spectral descriptors. Histogram Gradient Boosting (HGB) with spectral-only features ($R_λ$, K/S) and Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBDT) with recipe-process features outperforms other configurations with out-of-Fold MAE of 0.1655 and 0.1523 in the forward quality model. For inverse reconstruction, a component-wise median blend achieved a recipe-vector MAE of 0.0295. Exploratory conditional treatment effect (CATE) suggests an observational association that alkali adjustment reduces error for red and pale shades (CATE = -0.196). This framework provides a human-in-the-loop decision-support tool that minimizes costly laboratory trials across industrial formulation domains.

title: Normalized solutions to 1-Laplace equations with critical growth term
abstract: We study normalized solutions to the 1-Laplace equation \[ -div\left(Du{|Du|}\right)+λu{|u|}=f(u)+|u|^{1^*-2}u,\quadin~ R^N \] subject to the constraint int_{R^N}|u| , dx=m, where Ngeq2, 1^*=N{N-1} is the critical Sobolev exponent for the embedding from BV into L^p, λ, minR^+ and f:RtoR is a continuous nonlinear perturbation. We first establish a Pohozaev-type identity for the equation and use it to study the associated critical energy, and then prove the existence of normalized solutions via nonsmooth critical point theory. A key feature of our approach is the proof of the existence of a Palais-Smale sequence for a Lipschitz continuous functional under a Lipschitz continuous constraint. This is significantly different in methodology from previous problems with C^2 constraint.

title: LIVIN: Benchmarking Spatial and Embodied Intelligence in Digital Twins of Lived-In Homes
abstract: Realistic household simulation must capture not only diverse environments but also the lived-in object arrangements and spatial constraints that shape robot motion and interaction. Existing resources often trade off scale, real-world correspondence, and interaction readiness, leaving a gap in faithful, interactive replicas of how real homes are actually arranged. To this end, we introduce LIVIN, a benchmark for spatial and embodied intelligence built on digital twins of 30 diverse lived-in homes. These replicas preserve observed room layouts, furniture configurations, and everyday belongings. To construct them, we design a human-in-the-loop workflow comprising instance recognition, architectural reconstruction, and object generation and placement, with intermediate results reviewed and corrected by humans against the source observations at each stage. We evaluate four tasks in LIVIN: 3D detection, 3D reconstruction, navigation, and loco-manipulation. Our evaluations show that current methods remain challenged by the dense object arrangements, occlusions, limited free space, and constrained interaction regions found in realistic lived-in homes. We hope LIVIN will help advance embodied AI in real-world homes, from spatial understanding to robotic interaction, and ultimately bring embodied intelligence into everyday home environments.

title: Mine Odyssey: Benchmarking Spatial Agentic Intelligence in the Wild
abstract: Advances in foundation models are driving efforts to introduce agents to assist people in the physical world. Such agents require agentic spatial intelligence: exploring unfamiliar environments, updating spatial understanding through interaction, and adapting actions based on feedback to sustain progress toward a sequence of goals. Existing benchmarks cover only a limited range of spatial layouts, scales, and traversal requirements. We introduce Mine Odyssey, a benchmark for evaluating agentic spatial intelligence using Minecraft reconstructions of real-world locations. It comprises 180 tasks covering 30 such locations across 20 countries and regions on five continents, including 20 outdoor and 10 indoor settings. These settings span diverse spatial scales, layouts, terrains, and connectivity patterns, from Midtown Manhattan and rural Entrup to Santa Lucía Hill and Buckingham Palace. We select meaningful waypoints, such as landmarks, buildings, and rooms, and manually verify their accessibility. Each task provides a natural-language instruction specifying which waypoints to visit and in what order. Completing these tasks requires agents to find accessible routes and entrances, open doors, and move between levels using stairs and ladders, while monitoring their progress and recovering from navigation errors. Across eight evaluated state-of-the-art models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest success rate of 85.6%. However, the second-best model, Claude Opus 5.5, completes 73.9% of tasks, while the strongest evaluated open-weight model, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, reaches 23.9%, highlighting substantial room for improvement in the agentic spatial intelligence of current models. Comprehensive analyses and ablation studies on Mine Odyssey reveal current models' limitations and provide insights for advancing agentic spatial intelligence.

title: BlockSecML: A Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning Framework Using Homomorphic Encryption, Advanced Encryption Standard-256 (AES-256), and Blockchain
abstract: With machine learning being used more and more in sensitive areas like healthcare and finance, protecting the privacy of training data has become a serious concern.Most existing approaches handle encryption, secure computation, and audit logging as separate steps, which creates gaps where data can be exposed.In this paper, we present BlockSecML, a framework that brings together three technologies -Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)-256-Galois/Counter Mode encryption, Paillier partially homomorphic encryption (PHE), and Hyperledger Fabric blockchain -into a single working pipeline for privacy-preserving federated machine learning.The core design is as follows: gradient computation occurs entirely in plaintext at each data owner node; the computed gradients are immediately encrypted under Paillier PHE before any transmission; and the aggregation server performs homomorphic addition on the encrypted gradients without decrypting any individual contribution.Two brief in-memory plaintext windows exist at the data owner nodeduring local gradient computation and during AES-to-Paillier re-encoding -both of which are confined to the data owner's own device and do not involve network transmission.Every significant pipeline event is logged as an immutable, hash-chained record on a Hyperledger Fabric ledger.Experiments were conducted on an Intel Core i5-10210U laptop with 20 GB RAM.BlockSecML achieves classification accuracy of 97.6 ± 0.21% on MNIST (Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology), 84.9 ± 0.58% on MIMIC-III (Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care), and 91.7 ± 0.27% on a synthetic financial fraud dataset, compared to plaintext baselines of 98.9%, 87.2%, and 93.4%, respectively.Training time overhead ranges from 116% to 179% relative to plaintext training, with PHE computation accounting for approximately 87% of this overhead.All figures represent upper-bound estimates due to the single-machine experimental setup.Blockchain logging adds under 100 ms per round.The code is available at https://github.com/deeptisharda29/BlockSecML.

title: AIRP: uma arquitetura intermediária em linguagem natural estruturada para representação da intenção e orquestração adaptativa de investigações com modelos de linguagem
abstract: Este artigo apresenta o Adaptive Inference & Research Protocol (AIRP), uma arquitetura intermediária declarativa baseada em linguagem natural estruturada, desenvolvida para representar a intenção humana e organizar investigações complexas executadas por modelos de linguagem de grande porte (LLMs). A arquitetura integra compilação de intenção, preservação de restrições, estados epistemológicos, grafos investigativos, busca adaptativa, análise causal, tratamento de evidências e contradições, auditoria e condições de encerramento. O estudo apresenta os resultados de oito testes exploratórios comparando solicitações diretas (B0), prompts estruturados fortes (B1) e AIRP. As médias descritivas foram de 72,25, 93,25 e 96,38 pontos, respectivamente. O AIRP superou B1 em seis testes, empatou em um e apresentou resultado inferior em um. O artigo examina os resultados positivos e negativos, as limitações metodológicas e as questões de pesquisa parcialmente respondidas. Propõe, ainda, uma etapa confirmatória com avaliações independentes, replicações, ablações e métricas de custo computacional e esforço humano. Trata-se de uma contribuição arquitetural acompanhada de evidências experimentais exploratórias, sem alegação de superioridade estatisticamente comprovada. 10.5281/zenodo.23250028

title: RBE_Social_20000.
abstract: Dataset Analysis The dataset contains 20,000 synthetic Roman Bengali–English code-mixed conversational parallel text pairs designed for social-media-oriented text-to-English translation. The dataset was generated using conversational templates, Roman Bengali words/expressions, and their corresponding English equivalents, producing controlled variations of short conversational utterances. The source texts represent informal Roman Bengali–English code-mixed expressions commonly associated with social-media communication, while the target texts provide their corresponding English translations. The dataset is intended for research on code-mixed text normalization, language processing, machine translation, and Roman Bengali–English code-mixed-to-English translation, particularly in conversational and social-media contexts.

title: KC-Learner
abstract: Highlights KC-Learner v0.2.0 extends the project from a fixed reference experiment workflow toward reusable experimental infrastructure for sequential learner modeling and knowledge tracing. Added A canonical dataset contract for integrating external datasets after user-defined preprocessing. External learner-model adapter contracts for: psychometric streaming models; neural bundle-based models. A formal external experiment lifecycle with: TRAIN-only checkpoints; VALID replay verification; experiment freezing; explicit TEST authorization; TEST split commitment verification. Explicit dataset logical identity and dataset contract identity for reproducible external experiments. External implementation provenance and fingerprint requirements for formal reproducibility. Reference implementations KC-Learner continues to provide validated reference workflows for: Datasets EdNet-KT1 ASSISTments 2017 Learner models IRT AR-KT DKT-Q DKT-QC DKVMN-Q DKVMN-QC The existing reference execution, freeze, and evaluation semantics remain separate from the new external adapter workflow. Validation 200 automated tests pass in the release environment. Neural reference tests were executed with PyTorch and pykt-toolkit==0.0.38. The package builds successfully as both an sdist and a wheel. Extensibility External datasets are not automatically interpreted from arbitrary raw files. Users preprocess their data into the KC-Learner canonical interaction contract. External models must implement one of the documented KC-Learner adapter contracts. An arbitrary importable Python class is not sufficient for formal reproducible execution. Scope KC-Learner provides controlled and reproducible experimental execution under explicit dataset and model contracts. It does not guarantee that a learner model will achieve strong predictive performance or generalize equally well across datasets.

title: uqq-data
abstract: This dataset provides the data and computational materials supporting the article “Matrix-Based Source-Resolved Uncertainty Quantification for Pairwise Loss-Quantile Model Comparison” by Nidal Filali Baba and Ali El Myr. The archive contains Python scripts, saved simulation results, paired empirical loss-quantile profiles, source covariance matrices, training and evaluation splits, random seeds, execution metadata, software requirements, and verification routines. The experiments investigate severity-dependent ranking reversals, cancellation and amplification of shared uncertainty sources, finite-sample calibration, and the consequences of source interventions for model-selection certificates. The computational studies include controlled simulations, fitted neural comparisons involving Bayesian last-layer predictors and exact deep ensembles, and regression sensitivity experiments using the publicly available Diabetes dataset distributed with scikit-learn. The biomedical experiments use the s1 biomarker as the response and examine prespecified input, parameter, and response perturbations. The directories new_validation, ann_validation, and editorial_validation contain the reproducible validation studies. The directory data preserves numerical summaries from earlier complementary benchmarks; their original fitting scripts are not included. The accompanying README documents execution instructions, experimental scope, and reproducibility limitations.

title: A Catalytic Algorithm for Transposing Unknown Qutrit Unitaries with Tight Query Bounds
abstract: We construct exact deterministic circuits for transposing and inverting an unknown qutrit unitary $U\in\mathrm{SU}(3)$ using only forward queries. Three queries prepare a catalyst independently of the input state. Four further queries implement transposition while returning the catalyst unchanged and uncorrelated with the output. Two uses within an antisymmetric encoding implement inversion with eight processing queries and return the same catalyst. Reusing the catalyst implements $m$ transpositions or inversions with $3+4m$ or $3+8m$ total queries, respectively.
